notes: Slice 'concepts': the ideas of privacy (9 concept cards), an 18-regime comparison matrix (jurisdictions), 13 cases where records were turned on people (harms), and 8 popular myths. Method: every quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and checked with --check (FOUND) before being marked CONFIRMED; non-English quotes are given in the original with translations in note. Primary texts were preferred (statutes on official portals: publications.europa.eu Cellar for EUR-Lex texts, legislation.gov.uk, uscode.house.gov, govinfo.gov, Texas/Colorado legislature sites, camara.leg.br, npc.gov.cn, meity.gov.in, KLRI, sso.agc.gov.sg, legislation.gov.au, gov.za, ndpc.gov.ng, odpc.go.ke, fedlex; judgments from the BVerfG, Library of Congress U.S. Reports and the Third Circuit). Where a publisher blocked scripted access (EUR-Lex, consilium.europa.eu, projectvrm.org, some law-review repositories) an official mirror or an Internet Archive snapshot was used and the note says so. Field conventions: jurisdictions add 'automatedSignalsProvision' (the provision behind the yes/partial/no rating) and optional 'notes'; concepts add 'displayDate' and 'locationNote'. 'automatedSignals' = 'yes' only where the law obliges controllers to honour a person's automated or machine-readable objection/opt-out; 'partial' for registry-style opt-outs (Do Not Call lists) or consent intermediaries (India's Consent Managers). Known gaps and caveats: Westin's 1967 definition is quoted via Margulis (2003) because the book is in copyright; Nissenbaum is quoted from the 2004 pre-publication manuscript; Solove from a university-hosted copy of the published article. Unverified or approximate: CCPA's 1 Jan 2020 operative date, APPI's 2003/2005 dates and PIPA's 2011 entry-into-force are standard dates not confirmed on a primary page; the Colorado $20,000 penalty is from a law-firm advisory; Korea's 2026 PIPA amendment is from IAPP (secondary); the EU 'data omnibus' (proposed GDPR Art. 88b on machine-readable signals) was still in negotiation — its status at Sept 2026 was not verified from a primary source; Brazil's PL 2338/2023 status after March 2025 not verified. Harms not included for lack of a readable primary source: OPM breach 2015 (House Oversight report PDF is image-only beyond page 1), Grindr's 2018 sharing of HIV status (press only), Clearview AI fines by EU DPAs/ICO (sites blocked or pages withdrawn), the 23andMe Chapter 11 sale (company investor site blocked), Robodebt (Royal Commission site blocked), Target pregnancy-prediction anecdote (single anonymous source in a paywalled NYT article — treated as unverified and left out). The NYT AOL article is listed as PENDING (paywall, HTTP 403).

harms.place: U.S. Census Bureau / Department of Commerce, Washington, D.C.
harms.what: With confidentiality suspended by the Second War Powers Act of 1942, the Census Bureau released block-by-block data locating Japanese Americans and, in August 1943, gave the Secret Service the names and addresses of people of Japanese ancestry in the Washington, D.C., area.
harms.scale: About 112,000 people sent to 'assembly centers' between March and August 1942
harms.consequence: Nearly 70,000 of those removed were U.S. citizens, none charged with disloyalty; the Bureau's release of individual data was denied for decades until records surfaced in 2007.
